About Muyiwa Adekojede

I run paid media with research discipline.

I am a PPC specialist and paid acquisition operator. I help teams fix what is wasting budget, tighten conversion paths, and report performance in a way that is easy to verify.

SEO, writing, research, and teaching still shape my thinking, but paid media is where I spend most of my execution time now.

Current focus

I run PPC and paid acquisition work across Google Ads, Meta, TikTok, and adjacent channels.

Supporting foundations

SEO, writing, research, and teaching still shape how I make decisions and explain strategy.

I keep communication direct, reporting clear, and decisions tied to evidence you can inspect.

Based in Lagos, working internationally I work with teams that need cleaner acquisition systems, better measurement, and decisions that can hold up under review.

How the path shaped the work.

This is the sequence that matters most for context: where I started, what changed, and what now drives how I execute.

How I got here

I studied social work at the University of Lagos. That background taught me to pay attention to behaviour, context, and decision-making before I ever touched paid media.

I moved from writing into SEO delivery, then into campaign execution and paid acquisition. That route was not conventional, but it made my strategy work more grounded and practical.

What I focus on now

Most of my day-to-day work now sits in PPC, campaign management, measurement, and performance reporting.

SEO still matters in my process, but paid media is where I spend the most execution time.

What keeps the work sharp

Research and teaching keep me rigorous. They force me to justify assumptions and explain decisions clearly.

Writing helps for the same reason. If I cannot explain a campaign decision in plain language, I keep working until I can.

Publications and Research Output

I do not treat research as a publishing exercise. I use it to answer questions that matter and to build arguments I can defend with evidence.

My research examines consumer decision-making in complex, multi-channel environments. I investigate how people integrate information across touchpoints, how marketers can identify channel effectiveness, and how cultural factors shape those decisions in emerging markets.

This page collects my research agenda, methodologies, and current output across qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-method studies in healthcare systems, consumer behavior, and emerging-market research.

Years Active

Research Agenda

My research program centers on two connected themes: understanding consumer decision-making in multi-channel environments and developing better ways to measure marketing effectiveness in emerging markets.

They are not separate pursuits. Better understanding of consumer behavior improves measurement, and better measurement exposes gaps in how I understand behavior.

Consumer Journey Analytics & Multi-Touch Attribution

Most marketing operates in multi-channel environments. Consumers see your ad on Facebook, search on Google, read reviews, visit your site three times, then convert. Which touchpoint deserves credit? How do consumers actually integrate information across these channels?

Research Questions:

- How do consumers integrate information across digital touchpoints?

- What psychological mechanisms drive multi-touch attribution model performance?

- How can marketers causally identify channel effectiveness in observational data?

Methodological Approach:

Causal inference methods (experimental design, difference-in-differences), attribution modeling, machine learning for pattern identification in customer journey data.

Practical Application:

Building attribution models that reflect actual consumer decision-making processes, not just convenient mathematical formulas.

Consumer Behavior in Emerging Markets

Emerging markets aren't just "developing" markets with worse infrastructure. They're fundamentally different contexts where cultural schemas, institutional trust, and resource constraints shape consumer decision-making in unique ways.

- How do cultural schemas and institutional contexts shape consumer decision-making in resource-constrained environments?

- What drives innovation adoption when information is incomplete or contradictory?

- How do trust mechanisms operate differently across market contexts?

Mixed methods combining qualitative approaches (thematic analysis, interviews) with quantitative methods (surveys, quasi-experimental designs) to understand both mechanism and magnitude.

Marketing strategies that work in Western markets often fail in emerging markets - this research explains why and suggests adaptations.

Complete Publication List

Chronological listing of all research projects, publications, and academic work

Non-Conventional Uterotonics in Maternal Healthcare Systems: A Thematic Analysis

Muyiwa Adekojede / 2025 / University of Lagos

This study examines the prevalence and implications of herbal medicine use during childbirth in maternal healthcare systems. Through thematic analysis of interview data, we document how unclear dosing protocols contribute to post-partum complications including heavy bleeding and infections.

Election Observer Recommendations and Policy Implementation: A Multi-State Analysis

Multi-state qualitative study examining the implementation gap between election observer recommendations and actual institutional reforms. Analysis of transcripts from six states reveals systematic barriers to policy adoption and areas for institutional strengthening.

Drivers of Medical Device Reusage in Healthcare Settings: A Qualitative Investigation

Muyiwa Adekojede / 2024 / University of Lagos

This research investigates the cultural, financial, and institutional factors driving medical device reusage in healthcare facilities. Conducted following PLOS publication guidelines, the study reveals how trust in healthcare institutions and financial constraints shape device reuse practices.

Medical Devices Reusage Across Dual Healthcare Locations: Cultural and Institutional Factors

Undergraduate honors thesis examining medical device reusage practices across two different healthcare facility contexts. Mixed methods approach combining qualitative interviews and observational data reveals how cultural schemas, financial constraints, and institutional trust influence healthcare practices.

Determinants of Youth Drug Abuse: A Statistical Analysis of Peer Influence, Family Background, and Socio-Economic Factors

Muyiwa Adekojede / 2023 / University of Lagos

Comprehensive quantitative analysis of factors determining youth substance abuse patterns. Pearson correlation analysis of 200 respondents identified peer influence, family background, and socio-economic status as significant predictors (all p < 0.05).

Barriers to Prostate Cancer Screening: Demographics, Facility Availability, and Cost as Determinants

Muyiwa Adekojede (Statistical Supervisor) / 2023 / University of Lagos

Statistical analysis of prostate cancer screening adoption among 147 respondents. Chi-square analysis revealed that cost barriers (chi^2(2)=33.3763), facility availability (chi^2(2)=10.7736), and demographics (chi^2(2)=13.325) all significantly influence screening behavior.

Sexual Health Behaviors and Risk Factors: A Multi-Faculty University Study

Muyiwa Adekojede (Co-Researcher) / 2023 / University of Lagos

Large-scale quantitative research examining sexual health behaviors across university population (N=551). Chi-square analysis found no significant associations between social factors and risky sexual behaviors, suggesting complex multi-factorial determinants.

Mobile Payment Adoption and Digital Marketing Performance: The Mediating Role of Trust and Perceived Risk

Muyiwa Adekojede / 2025 / Independent Study

Ongoing independent research examining how trust perceptions and risk assessments influence mobile payment adoption among Nigerian youth. Study integrates digital marketing performance metrics to understand the relationship between payment system preferences and online engagement.

Research Streams

Healthcare Systems & Qualitative Research

Research focusing on healthcare practices, device reusage, maternal health, and healthcare decision-making in emerging markets. Emphasis on qualitative methodologies (thematic analysis, interview methods) to understand the "why" behind healthcare behaviors.

Key Insight: Healthcare providers in resource-constrained settings make rational decisions given institutional constraints - policy interventions must address those constraints, not just provider behavior.

Consumer Behavior & Quantitative Analysis

Quantitative investigations of consumer decision-making patterns, behavioral determinants, and statistical analysis of risk factors and protective factors across populations.

Key Insight: Consumer behaviors are multi-factorial - single-variable explanations (e.g., "it's all about price") rarely hold up under rigorous statistical testing.

Digital Marketing & Consumer Adoption

Research examining digital marketing adoption, mobile payment systems, online consumer behavior, and the role of trust and perceived risk in technology adoption.

Key Insight: Trust and perceived risk aren't just "nice to have" - they're fundamental mediators of consumer adoption decisions in digital environments.

Institutional Analysis

Qualitative analysis of institutional processes, policy implementation, governance structures, and the gap between recommendations and actual reforms in organizational contexts.

Key Insight: Institutional change requires addressing political and structural barriers, not just technical improvements.

pages.text:
How to Find the Latest Google Patents Related to SEO

If anyone is as curious as me and, you know, from time to time you might have wondered how to get information about the latest patent search engine related papers which have been released by search engines such as Google, Bing, Yandex. But I am much focused on google patent search engine related papers since the search engine currently accounts for 91.47 percent of global search traffic, according to Statista . That means more than 90% of people in the world use Google.

So first, I went through the social accounts of Google and Bing, trying to see if from time to time, things about patents related to search engine results optimization are published there. What I found is that little or nothing about this has been, you know, published by their social media pages. It's not even about that; it's about me (and probably you too) trying to get the latest information on the latest patents in the SEO field - because that increases your knowledge you know. I mean this papers hold information that are like goldmines. So why not chase to find and read them at all costs? So, I had to do a much deeper dive myself into the search engine results pages. I needed answers.

How I Find the Latest Google Search Engine Optimization-focused Patents

I'll be explaining how I found to easily search and discover latest search engine optimization-focused patents on Google patent website and how you can implement that approach so you get to stay in the loop of latest information. This way, you can always work with that information and stay steadfast in your tasks or practices as SEO specialists .

How to Filter and Use Google Patents Advanced Search Page

So, if you're interested, go to the Google Patents website at patent.google.com . On the homepage, you'll see three icons in the search bar. Below the search bar is a tick box labeled "Include non-patent literature (Google Scholar)," but you won't need that. Instead, focus on the three icons in the search bar: the first one resembles a bulb, the second a graduation cap, and the third a filter icon. Click on the filter icon, and it will immediately take you to another page. This is called the Google Patents Advanced Search Page .

Now, let's say you want to see the latest patents by Google related to search engine results and others. On the google advanced patent search page, go to the "Assign" section, type "Google Incorporation" (it'll be abbreviated to "Inc."), and fill in the date range. Next, select "Priority" from the dropdown menu, which includes all together "Priority," "Filing," and "Publication."

What are "Priority," "Filing," and "Publication" in Google Patent

Now, it's important to understand these terms. The "Priority" date is essentially the first time a patent was filed, whether domestically or internationally. This is different from when it was published, as it marks the initial filing with the local jurisdiction, securing the inventor's rights. For example, if Google invents a new type of phone case and files a provisional application on January 1, 2023, this date becomes their priority date. However, filing a full patent application can later be in 2024 and that would not affect or change the initial priority date.

Meaning of When a Patent Claims Priority

When a patent claims priority, it essentially means the inventor is using the date of filing as the starting point for patent rights. 6 Types of Duplicate Content According to Google's Patent

Okay, so this paper called Detecting Query-Specific Duplicate Tokens is a patent by Google. And basically what this paper is all about is that it outlines the pattern of ways in which Google can use to detect duplicated documents. And then it knows how to find the unoriginal content or duplicated content and then use the best mechanics to display only relevant documents on the search engine result page.

How Google Process Search Results to Filter Out Duplicate Content

Below are the steps search engines like google can detect duplicate contents and only show users relevant results when they make a query on the search page.

Step One: User Enters a Query

So the first step, of course, is when the client goes into the search engine and puts in the query. Let's say they put in a search term called "best coffee shops near me."

Search Engine Analyzes the Query

And then what the search engine will do is it will take in this result, take in this term, and then try to check its own reposition. And then take this term into its repository and then try to see which tokens are most relevant to this term.

Grouping Relevant Documents

After, it tries to group the documents relevant to this term. Let's say somebody searches about "best coffee shops near me" in the UK or in New York, it, it tends to group them based on the query.

Extraction of Relevant Snippets from Documents

The next thing for it to do is that it looks into each document and then looks at the most relevant part of the document that best serves the query to which the person or the user has re-positioned. This extraction of important pieces of text is called snippets.

Compression and Grouping Relevant Snippets

It then moves into the fifth stage, which is going to compress the document. So this relevant part, which it has drawn out from the stage 4, it tries to group them. And the reason why it's grouping them, let's say there is a document called "document A" and it has this "best coffee shops near me" information which is relevant to the query. Document B also has this "best coffee shops near me" information which is relevant to the query.

Filtering Out Duplicate Content

After it has gotten this snippet, which is the relevant permission it has drawn from each document, it then tries to see which one has the most similarity or which one leaves gaps. So based on these categorization of those relevant snippets, it tries to compare which are identical or similar. So whichever is identical and not authentic on its own, it tends to filter them out. This duplicate can be of different types (more on that below).

Prevention of Duplicate Results for Improved User Experience

Then in the next step, after it has filtering out the duplicates, the search engine ranks the relevant documents in the search result page. And the reason why the system does all these (from stage one to 6) is because of user experience - to prevents the case where they need to go through ten links on Google which most of them seem alike.

Types of Duplicated Content According to Google Patent

So, this patent mentions six different types of duplicates, though it didn't attribute a defined term used to explain each duplicate. It used diagrams, like from figure 1 to figure 6, so six different figures. So, I mentioned each figure, and then sought to explain each duplicate denoted by a figure. And then I try to give them a better name so you can easily understand what each duplicate means, even at first glance.

Figure 1: An Expanded Duplicate

For Fig. 1, I called name it "Expanded Duplicate." This diagram contains two documents - the first document and the second document. So, as you can see (figure 1 in the image attached), the second document contains or encapsulates every bit and part of the first document. Moreso, you will notice that the writer of the second document went out of their way to include "a bit extra information" of what the first document does not.

Figure 2: A Partial Overlapping Duplicates

For the second figure, I call this a "Partial Overlap Duplicate." When you check figure 2 in the image, you will see that both documents in that type of duplicate have similar content - but it doesn't end there. Even as each has similar content, the writers for both documents went out of their way to research to provide information that is unique to both documents ensuring that each piece of info covers a particular aspect or topic that the other (writer) does not.

Figure 3: A Minimal Common Duplicate

Moving on to Fig. 3, I call this a "Minimal Common Duplicate." In this case, the two different documents have some information in common. Document A and Document B each contain sections that are common to both, but it's not necessarily the entirety of either document. This means a large part of each document is unique, with only a few differentiating common elements, which is why I call it a "Minimal Common Duplicate."

Figure 4: An Embedded Duplicate

For Fig. 4, the first document contains all the content of the second document and a significant amount of additional information. So, for figure 4, you can see that document A entirely consumes document B. And document B, which is consumed by document A, is below 50% size of document A. So, to use a real life scenario to describe this, imagine a big publisher like Yahoo News or BBC News, and then they publish a particular news story, and then a very small publisher website or a new publisher website just goes on that page, and they just copy half part of that document and they publish it. So, in essence, the first document or document A, which is from BBC, totally encapsulates the smaller version of information because the second or small publisher only picked few exact information from the document A here, which is the document from BBC. This is why I call it an "Embedded Duplicate."

Figure 5: A Contextual Duplicate

For Fig. 5, I call this a "Contextual Duplicate." Here, document A and document B both have a little bit of information about Company X. In real-life context, imagine a news story from the BBC (Document A) about a release of product about Company X and the news story from the small publisher (Document b), in this case, the small publisher doesn't entirely take a chunk about company X product release from the BBC's article, but only a very little part. Let's say the small publisher takes a small precise information about the product release from the news story from the BBC, and then they try to develop that with other information that they can get online or from the staffs of company X. So, in the very end, when this comes up in the search results, you'll see that probably the title or even a small part of the body might be the same thing. For this can be in form of qoutes.

Figure 6: An Embedded Contextual Duplicate

Finally, for Fig. 6, which is the last kind of duplicate, I will call it an "Embedded Contextual Duplicate." Looking at the earlier diagram, you can see CompanyX was also used for illustration, but in a slightly different way. I also explain this using a real-life scenario that covers CompanyX (precisely its biography) and how its founder came to be. The Document B could be written by a BBC journalist who focused solely on the history of CompanyX.. As for Document A, it was written and published by a writer at Wikipedia detailing not only how CompanyX came about but also how its CEO grew from the grassroots to founding the company.

Best Web 2.0 Practices for Quality Link Building (+40 Free Web 2.0 Websites in 2025)

Link building includes guest posts, link insertions, web 2.0, comment linking, local citations, image submissions, social bookmarking, branded networks, and PR releases.

This document, however, covers only one of them: Web 2.0.

The document outlines the guiding principles for creating quality web 2.0 links, the checklist for easy creation, and the do's and don'ts. In addition, it presents a list of the top web 2.0 websites that accept web 2.0 publications.

Web 2.0 Guidelines: What NOT to Do When Publishing Content

1. Don't Publish the Same Content on Different Web 2.0 Platforms

Rather, rephrase the first content, leaving the keyword intact.

You can use a one-line prompt in ChatGPT to rewrite or rephrase the first piece of content you created for your web 2.0.

2. Distribute Web 2.0s Across Multiple Platforms, Not a Single Platform

The primary emphasis is on diversifying content across multiple platforms rather than creating multiple content on the same platform. More often than not, when publishers are requested to publish on platforms, they go on a spree to publish ten different content on one single platform, e.g., Medium, at a go. But that is not what I request them to do. What I request rather is that they post each among the ten content on ten different platforms. So that's one content per platform. Each platform has its unique audience and purpose, so spreading content across various platforms ensures broader reach and engagement.

Here's an analogy that helps explain better: You have ten delicious dishes you want to share. You wouldn't put all ten on a single plate, would you? You'd serve each dish on appropriate plates – a pizza on a platter, soup in a bowl, and so on.

Below, this publisher published different content on only Medium.

3. Don't Publish Twice on a Web 2.0 Accepting Platform

This can easily lead to the account getting banned. So please desist from publishing Web 2.0s on only one platform.

When a publisher posts a Web 2.0 twice or more on a platform, he/she is no longer doing Web 2.0. It is then called Spamming. Often, this infuriates the admin of Web 2.0-accepting platforms such as Substack, leading them to delete the account and label it as spamming.

In the end, Google will also get the "hint" that such content and links in the content deleted are not relevant.

4. Don't Use One Image for Every Web 2.0 Content You Publish

For example, an intern used the same image for every web 2.0 piece he published throughout the week. He continued the same thing the next week. I advised him to stop such practice because the web 2.0 content published must appear unique and be genuine, not like duplicates.

5. Don't Link Only on Secondary Keywords

As you can see, Images 3.1 and 3.2 are taken from the same content. Two different terms or phrases are hyperlinked, but neither is the primary keyword given to this web 2.0 content writer. The primary keyword given was "classic car." Now, that term wasn't hyperlinked in the content.

Please try not to make a similar mistake. Hyperlink on the primary keyword once, then diversify the hyperlinking to other terms you are working with or targeting.

6. Don't Do a Train of Links

Don't use complete sentence(s) as anchor text.

Sometimes, glitches might occur on a publishing website, so things might not go according to their meaning. In the image of the case study shown above, interlinking didn't go well. Rather than proper interlinking, there's a train of links that circles almost the entire body paragraph. The publisher is expected to correct this by all means necessary. This is because the essence of interlinking a word term is to:

For users to discover related topics which will improve user experience

To signal relevance to search engines

Improves ranking potential

For search engines to understand website structure

Web 2.0 Best Practices: What TO DO for Quality Link Building

1. Use Google Images for Your Web 2.0 Content

Just paste your keyword into Google and download or copy an image relevant to the keyword.

2. One Keyword Per Content

For instance, if you are given a series of keywords to create web 2.0 targeting a particular page, use one per day. Don't stuff all keywords into one content at the same time.

For instance, you can use "vintage car racing" for today and "classic car events" for tomorrow. Follow that pattern. Don't cram five different keywords into one piece of content, like a food vendor forcing vegetables, sliced cheese, and meat into a sandwich.

3. Interlink Only on Your Primary Keyword

At all times, you must also ensure you interlink only your primary keyword (except when you have a primary and secondary keyword, in which case you interlink both) in the content body paragraph, not in the subheadings or title.

Diversify Your Backlinks

Forget the old rule of focusing on a single primary keyword for interlinking your web 2.0s. That approach can hurt your SEO as Google frowns upon manipulative backlink strategies. When you have a variety of anchor texts that make your backlink profile look natural, you avoid raising red flags.

Don't just interlink with one exact keyword. You should interlink with a variety of keywords. So ideally, you should be given a primary keyword and other synonyms. You should interlink once or at most twice on the primary keyword. Other types of interlinking should occur on synonyms or branded anchors (e.g., company name), or generic terms similar to the primary keyword (e.g., "cleaning solutions"), and or long-tail phrases similar to the primary key term ("best eco-friendly cleaning services"). You can also make good use of Navigational with Keywords (e.g., Get your home cleaned by CleanFreaks). In times when you've exhausted all the latter, feel free to interlink to the naked URL.

4. Your Primary Keyword Must Be in Your Title

Your keyword should always be or make up your content title, not something else. Preferably, the keyword should be at the beginning of your title.

In the case above, the keyword assigned for the content is "vintage motoring". That should be in your title, not "classic car myths" or "classic cars".

5. Only Interlink Your Keyword in the Body Paragraph

Usually, you should work with only one primary keyword to avoid dilution or confusion when search engines like Google or Bing parse the web 2.0 content. This interlinking should only occur in the body of the content.

As you can see, this is published web 2.0 content with the primary keyword "business coaching services in London". You'll note that only "Business coaching" is used in their title. This can lead to the content being shown by Google to readers who aren't the target audience. As you can see, the primary keyword targets the audience in London, UK. However, only "Business coaching" will mean search engines won't know that the content is targeted at people in the UK and, therefore, won't show the keyword to people in the UK.

Therefore, you should have "business coaching services in London" in your title, not just "Business coaching."

Again, only interlink your keyword in the article.

7. Don't Forget to Publish the Newly Created WordPress Site

In case you use WordPress's free website service to create web 2.0, take note that WordPress, even after fully creating all aspects of the site that are needed, requires you to publish the site. If you don't, the site will remain in Draft mode and not live.

To solve this, just go to the wp-admin panel of the site (WordPress) and publish the draft version of the site itself.

8. Create Brand Name Accounts on Web 2.0 Websites

It is imperative that you create a brand name account for the brand you are targeting and publish on it. It's not a good idea to create a personal account and publish on that. When web 2.0 content gets indexed and displayed on SERP, (if the account used to publish is the brand name) the brand name will appear along with the web 2.0 content, which looks more credible than when random named accounts are used. In the example below, the publisher published on a personal account.

In this case, the platform used is Quora. The publisher used their name to create a personal profile which the web 2.0s are published on. What is advised here is that the publisher creates a "Space" on Quora with the brand name, e.g., "Corporate Removal Group's Space" and publishes the web 2.0s on that.

Step-by-Step Checklist for Web 2.0 Creation

One or two, or more of the steps below must not be skipped.

Have a keyword

Have a target URL

Use keywords to create content (e.g., with ChatGpt, Bard, Claude, etc.)

Rephrase content into the number of links you are to produce for the day

Do interlink in the content created

Interlink only on the keyword

Ensure your H1, H2, H3, H4, etc. are well structured

Include an image in your content

Go over and edit the content through (X2)

Create an account on a web 2.0-accepting platform, e.g., Blogger or Medium

blocks.text: Best Web 2.0 Practices for Quality Link Building (+40 Free Web 2.0 Websites in 2025)
Link building includes guest posts, link insertions, web 2.0, comment linking, local citations, image submissions, social bookmarking, branded networks, and PR releases.
This document, however, covers only one of them: Web 2.0.

The document outlines the guiding principles for creating quality web 2.0 links, the checklist for easy creation, and the do's and don'ts. In addition, it presents a list of the top web 2.0 websites that accept web 2.0 publications.
Web 2.0 Guidelines: What NOT to Do When Publishing Content
1. Don't Publish the Same Content on Different Web 2.0 Platforms
Rather, rephrase the first content, leaving the keyword intact.
You can use a one-line prompt in ChatGPT to rewrite or rephrase the first piece of content you created for your web 2.0.
2. Distribute Web 2.0s Across Multiple Platforms, Not a Single Platform

The primary emphasis is on diversifying content across multiple platforms rather than creating multiple content on the same platform. More often than not, when publishers are requested to publish on platforms, they go on a spree to publish ten different content on one single platform, e.g., Medium, at a go. But that is not what I request them to do. What I request rather is that they post each among the ten content on ten different platforms. So that's one content per platform. Each platform has its unique audience and purpose, so spreading content across various platforms ensures broader reach and engagement.

Here's an analogy that helps explain better: You have ten delicious dishes you want to share. You wouldn't put all ten on a single plate, would you? You'd serve each dish on appropriate plates – a pizza on a platter, soup in a bowl, and so on.
Below, this publisher published different content on only Medium.
3. Don't Publish Twice on a Web 2.0 Accepting Platform
This can easily lead to the account getting banned. So please desist from publishing Web 2.0s on only one platform.

When a publisher posts a Web 2.0 twice or more on a platform, he/she is no longer doing Web 2.0. It is then called Spamming. Often, this infuriates the admin of Web 2.0-accepting platforms such as Substack, leading them to delete the account and label it as spamming.
In the end, Google will also get the "hint" that such content and links in the content deleted are not relevant.
4. Don't Use One Image for Every Web 2.0 Content You Publish

For example, an intern used the same image for every web 2.0 piece he published throughout the week. He continued the same thing the next week. I advised him to stop such practice because the web 2.0 content published must appear unique and be genuine, not like duplicates.
5. Don't Link Only on Secondary Keywords

As you can see, Images 3.1 and 3.2 are taken from the same content. Two different terms or phrases are hyperlinked, but neither is the primary keyword given to this web 2.0 content writer. The primary keyword given was "classic car." Now, that term wasn't hyperlinked in the content.
Please try not to make a similar mistake. Hyperlink on the primary keyword once, then diversify the hyperlinking to other terms you are working with or targeting.
6. Don't Do a Train of Links
Don't use complete sentence(s) as anchor text.

Sometimes, glitches might occur on a publishing website, so things might not go according to their meaning. In the image of the case study shown above, interlinking didn't go well. Rather than proper interlinking, there's a train of links that circles almost the entire body paragraph. The publisher is expected to correct this by all means necessary. This is because the essence of interlinking a word term is to:
For users to discover related topics which will improve user experience
To signal relevance to search engines
Improves ranking potential
For search engines to understand website structure
Web 2.0 Best Practices: What TO DO for Quality Link Building
1. Use Google Images for Your Web 2.0 Content
Just paste your keyword into Google and download or copy an image relevant to the keyword.
2. One Keyword Per Content
For instance, if you are given a series of keywords to create web 2.0 targeting a particular page, use one per day. Don't stuff all keywords into one content at the same time.

For instance, you can use "vintage car racing" for today and "classic car events" for tomorrow. Follow that pattern. Don't cram five different keywords into one piece of content, like a food vendor forcing vegetables, sliced cheese, and meat into a sandwich.
3. Interlink Only on Your Primary Keyword

At all times, you must also ensure you interlink only your primary keyword (except when you have a primary and secondary keyword, in which case you interlink both) in the content body paragraph, not in the subheadings or title.
Diversify Your Backlinks

Forget the old rule of focusing on a single primary keyword for interlinking your web 2.0s. That approach can hurt your SEO as Google frowns upon manipulative backlink strategies. When you have a variety of anchor texts that make your backlink profile look natural, you avoid raising red flags.

Don't just interlink with one exact keyword. You should interlink with a variety of keywords. So ideally, you should be given a primary keyword and other synonyms. You should interlink once or at most twice on the primary keyword. Other types of interlinking should occur on synonyms or branded anchors (e.g., company name), or generic terms similar to the primary keyword (e.g., "cleaning solutions"), and or long-tail phrases similar to the primary key term ("best eco-friendly cleaning services"). You can also make good use of Navigational with Keywords (e.g., Get your home cleaned by CleanFreaks). In times when you've exhausted all the latter, feel free to interlink to the naked URL.
4. Your Primary Keyword Must Be in Your Title
Your keyword should always be or make up your content title, not something else. Preferably, the keyword should be at the beginning of your title.
In the case above, the keyword assigned for the content is "vintage motoring". That should be in your title, not "classic car myths" or "classic cars".
5. Only Interlink Your Keyword in the Body Paragraph

Usually, you should work with only one primary keyword to avoid dilution or confusion when search engines like Google or Bing parse the web 2.0 content. This interlinking should only occur in the body of the content.

As you can see, this is published web 2.0 content with the primary keyword "business coaching services in London". You'll note that only "Business coaching" is used in their title. This can lead to the content being shown by Google to readers who aren't the target audience. As you can see, the primary keyword targets the audience in London, UK. However, only "Business coaching" will mean search engines won't know that the content is targeted at people in the UK and, therefore, won't show the keyword to people in the UK.
Therefore, you should have "business coaching services in London" in your title, not just "Business coaching."
Again, only interlink your keyword in the article.
7. Don't Forget to Publish the Newly Created WordPress Site

In case you use WordPress's free website service to create web 2.0, take note that WordPress, even after fully creating all aspects of the site that are needed, requires you to publish the site. If you don't, the site will remain in Draft mode and not live.
To solve this, just go to the wp-admin panel of the site (WordPress) and publish the draft version of the site itself.
8. Create Brand Name Accounts on Web 2.0 Websites

It is imperative that you create a brand name account for the brand you are targeting and publish on it. It's not a good idea to create a personal account and publish on that. When web 2.0 content gets indexed and displayed on SERP, (if the account used to publish is the brand name) the brand name will appear along with the web 2.0 content, which looks more credible than when random named accounts are used. In the example below, the publisher published on a personal account.

In this case, the platform used is Quora. The publisher used their name to create a personal profile which the web 2.0s are published on. What is advised here is that the publisher creates a "Space" on Quora with the brand name, e.g., "Corporate Removal Group's Space" and publishes the web 2.0s on that.

So you're looking for an International SEO expert who actually delivers results. Maybe your site isn't showing up on Google. Maybe your competitors are getting all the traffic. Or maybe you just know something's not working, but you're not sure what.

What I'm NOT Going to Do

I'm not going to promise you first-page rankings by next Tuesday. I'm not going to throw around words like "dominate" or tell you I have some secret Google connection. And I'm definitely not going to overcharge you when you're a small business just trying to grow.

What I WILL Do

I'll help you rank for keywords that actually bring customers. I'll fix the technical issues that are killing your site. And I'll do it with the kind of transparency and dedication you won't find at most agencies.

My Track Record as an International SEO Expert:

As an International SEO expert who's worked across six continents, I've built a reputation for delivering measurable results:

So if you're serious about actually growing your online presence, not just "exploring options," keep reading.

International SEO Service Mistakes: Why Language Translation Isn't Enough

Let me tell you about a mistake I made early on. I was working on international SEO for a tech product, and I thought I had everything figured out. Set up the site, added some translations, threw in the hreflang tags the way some blog post told me to. Easy, right?

Weeks went by. The site wasn't ranking in any of the target countries. And it wasn't until I dug into the Google documentation on hreflang that I realized I'd set it up completely wrong.

The Real Truth About International SEO

Here's what most businesses get wrong about international SEO: they think it's just about language. It's not. It's about location, culture, search behavior, and yeah, even which search engine people actually use in that country.

The Three Biggest Mistakes I See on Websites

Misusing hreflang tags

Even professional developers mess this up. I've seen it on sites built by agencies charging thousands. When you get it wrong, Google gets confused about which version to show to which users.

Ignoring internal links

I once worked on a site with over 50,000 URLs. You know how many internal links most had? Zero. None. The site was a ghost town with no roads connecting anything.

Assuming 'fast' is good enough

Your site might load okay, but 'okay' doesn't cut it anymore. Google's pushing Core Web Vitals hard, and if your site isn't fast by their standards, you're losing rankings.

Is Your Business Ready for International SEO?

Required Budget, Timeline, and Others

Look, I'm going to be upfront here. SEO isn't for every business at every stage. And I'm not going to take your money if I know it won't work.

Here's when I'll tell you "not yet":

Budget Not Ready

If you're not ready to invest what it actually takes, I'll quietly move on. SEO requires consistent effort over months, and that means committing real resources. If the budget isn't there yet, that's okay -- but I'd rather be honest about it upfront.

Won't Invest in Content

SEO and content go hand-in-hand. You can't optimize what doesn't exist. And no, AI-generated fluff doesn't count—Google's getting very good at detecting and penalizing that .

Need Results Too Fast

If you need something done in the next few weeks, SEO probably isn't your answer. It takes 3-6 months to see solid results . Anyone who guarantees first-page rankings in 30 days is lying.

My Comprehensive International SEO Services for Small to Enterprise Businesses

Technical SEO Services: Site Audits, Speed Optimization, and Crawlability

Technical SEO services are where I find the stuff that's quietly killing your rankings. And trust me, there's always something.

I had a client once—a logistics company—and their site kept on with Zeros in rankings. They'd tried everything: new content, new search engine marketing specialist, and even redesigned the whole site. Nothing worked.

I ran technical SEO services to audit the site and found double slashes in their URL structure. Sounds minor, right? It wasn't. Google was treating every URL as two separate pages. Their whole site was essentially duplicate content in Google's eyes.

What a Proper Technical Audit Covers:

Crawlability check: Can Google even access your pages?

XML sitemap: Is it submitted? Is it actually accurate? Will Google get pinged when a new page goes live?

Robots.txt: Are you accidentally blocking important pages?

Page speed: Using tools like PageSpeed Insights to find every single thing slowing you down

Mobile responsiveness: Over 60% of searches happen on mobile. If your site doesn't work there, you're done.

Structured data: Helps Google understand what your content actually is

HTTPS and security: Non-secure sites get penalized. Period.

I document everything, prioritize what actually matters, and give you a roadmap you can follow.

On-Page SEO: Headers, Meta Tags, and Content Optimization

On-page search engine optimization is about making each page as relevant as possible for the keywords you're targeting.

And this is where I see the most mistakes. Let me give you an example: I was doing a consultation for a tech company, and I looked at their header tag structure. They had H4s and H3s at the start of the page. Then H1s and H2s at the end.

That's like writing a book where you put chapter titles at the end of each chapter. It confuses readers, and it confuses Google.

What Proper On-Page SEO Involves:

Best On-Page SEO Tools: Extensions and Platforms I Use Daily

• Detailed SEO Extension - Get SEO insights at the click of a button to any website you're currently on.

• Link Redirect Trace - Perform advanced, comprehensive, and correct analysis of redirects and REL-canonicals.

• SEO Search Simulator - Simulate search engine queries from any location on Google and easily check and track your website or your competitor's rankings.

• SEOquake - Provides you with key SEO metrics, along with other useful tools such as SEO Audit, and many others.

• Semrush - Drive growth in SEO, PPC, content, social media, and traffic for most marketing projects.

• Ahrefs Webmaster Tool - Scans website for common technical & on-page SEO issues.

• Google Search Console - Provides reports to help you measure your site's Search traffic and performance.

Link Building Services: Quality Backlinks Without Spam Tactics

Links are still one of Google's top ranking factors. But link building in 2025 is not what it was in 2015.

Here's a story: I was working with an eCommerce store, and they wanted to rank for competitive keywords fast. Someone told them about Fiverr—you could buy 100 backlinks for $5. Sounded great, right?

Those links? They came from spam sites, random blog comments, and link farms. Within weeks, Google penalized the site. Their rankings tanked. Traffic disappeared. And fixing that mess takes months longer than if they'd just done it right from the start.

How I Actually Build Links:

I focus on quality over quantity . One link from a respected industry publication is worth more than 100 links from random directories.

I use guest posts on relevant sites . Not just any site that'll take content—sites your target audience actually reads.

I do broken link building . Find broken links on authoritative sites, create content that replaces what died, reach out to suggest they update to your link.

And I absolutely avoid anything that looks like a scheme . Google's spam policies are very clear on this. If you're buying links, using private blog networks, or doing anything shady, you will get caught. Maybe not today. But eventually.

SEO Content Strategy: Human-Written vs AI-Generated Content

As an SEO expert, let me be very clear about something: AI-generated content is a problem.

I've seen so many businesses try to replace their writers with ChatGPT or whatever tool. And every single time, it backfires. The content is fluffy. It says a lot of words without actually saying anything. And Google can detect it.

When you publish AI content without human review and editing, Google can penalize your site . I've watched sites lose 60%, 80%, even 90% of their organic traffic because they tried to game the system with mass-produced AI content.

My Approach: Human-Written Content Backed by Research and Strategy

I work with content writers who actually understand the topics they're writing about. I create content that provides genuine value, not just keyword-stuffed articles designed to trick Google.

Every piece of content has a purpose: to answer a question, solve a problem, or guide someone toward making a decision. That's what ranks. That's what converts.

Local SEO Services

Local SEO services are critical if you have a physical location or serve a specific geographic area.

I've worked with businesses in over 60 countries across six continents, so I've seen how local SEO works in wildly different markets—from Lagos to London to Singapore.

What Local SEO Involves:

Google Business Profile (GBP): This is your Google Maps listing. If you're not showing up here, you're invisible to local searchers. I help you set this up properly, optimize it with the right categories and keywords, and create a posting schedule to keep it active.

Local citations: These are mentions of your business name, address, and phone number across the web. Consistency matters. If your address is written differently on different sites, Google gets confused.

Review management: Good reviews help you rank. Bad reviews? They hurt, but they're not the end of the world if you respond professionally. No reviews? That's worse than bad reviews.

Location-based pages: If you serve multiple cities, each location needs its own optimized page with unique content about that specific area.

I've helped businesses rank for "[service] near me" searches, which are huge for local visibility. And the best part? Local SEO is usually less competitive than national SEO, so you can see results faster.

WordPress SEO Services: Speed, Plugins, and Technical Optimization

As a WordPress SEO specialist, I've been working with WordPress for over four years, and I've seen some sites that made me shake my head.

I once consulted for a Singapore business using DIVI theme. They'd built this beautiful site, hired designers, spent a ton of money. But when I looked under the hood? The SEO was a disaster. Their homepage was loading at 8 seconds. They had no proper title tags. Their images were massive and not optimized. Almost half of their website was basically invisible to Google.

What WordPress SEO Involves:

Initial setup: Connecting Google Search Console and Google Analytics from day one. You need data. Without it, you're flying blind.

Plugins: I use RankMath , Yoast , or All in One SEO for on-page optimization. Link Whisper for internal linking. Smush and Imagify for compressing images without losing quality.

Speed optimization: WordPress sites can get slow fast. I use tools like WP Rocket and NitroPack to make sure your site loads in under 2 seconds.

Theme selection: Some themes are beautiful but terrible for SEO. I help you pick themes that are both good-looking and technically sound.

Enterprise SEO Services

Enterprise SEO is different. You're dealing with thousands of pages, complex site structures, multiple teams, and high stakes.

My Five-Pillar Approach:

You need to know exactly what's working at scale.

At enterprise level, small technical issues multiply into huge problems.

You can't manually optimize 10,000 pages. You need systems.

Building and maintaining domain authority at scale.

Moving enterprise sites without losing rankings requires meticulous planning.

I've helped brands migrate thousands of URLs without traffic loss. I've built content workflows that produced consistent results across multiple markets. And I've worked on sites where a 1% improvement in conversion rate meant millions in revenue.

Google's Global Rankings System for All Businesses Online (Through International SEO)

Here's something most people don't get about international SEO : Google doesn't just look at your content and decide whether to rank you everywhere. It looks at specific signals to figure out which country's search results you should appear in.

If you get these signals wrong? You could rank perfectly in one country while being completely invisible in another.

Technical SEO Audit Service

I use technical SEO audits to surface the issues that quietly suppress rankings: crawl waste, rendering problems, redirect chains, slow templates, indexation mistakes, and mobile UX failures.

You get a prioritized audit, evidence for each issue, and a clear explanation of what needs fixing now versus what can wait.

What's Included in Your Technical SEO Audit

Comprehensive website analysis covering the technical factors that impact rankings, crawlability, and user experience.

Site Crawlability & Indexation Analysis

Identify crawl errors, broken links, redirect chains, and indexation issues preventing search engines from properly accessing your content. You'll know exactly which pages aren't being crawled and why.

Core Web Vitals & Page Speed Assessment

Measure Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), First Input Delay (FID), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). Identify what's slowing down your site and get specific fixes to improve loading speed.

Mobile Usability Evaluation

Test mobile-friendliness, responsive design issues, tap target sizing, and mobile page speed. Google prioritizes mobile-first indexing, so mobile problems tank your rankings.

Site Architecture Review

Analyze URL structure, internal linking, navigation hierarchy, and XML sitemap quality. Poor site architecture confuses search engines and buries important pages.

Schema Markup & Structured Data Audit

Security & HTTPS Assessment

Verify SSL certificate implementation, mixed content issues, and security headers. Non-HTTPS sites get penalized in rankings and scare away visitors.

Duplicate Content Detection

Robots.txt & Meta Robots Analysis

Prioritized Fix Roadmap

60%+ of searches happen on mobile

Pages Google can't access won't rank

Dilutes ranking power across multiple URLs

Seeing Traffic Drops Without Clear Reason

Before going live with a new site or major redesign, identify technical problems that'll hurt rankings. Catching issues pre-launch is 10x easier than fixing them after launch.

SEO Investment Not Delivering Results

You're creating content, building links, doing "all the right things" but rankings aren't improving. Technical issues might be blocking everything else from working.

Your site has been live for years but never had a comprehensive technical review. Accumulated technical debt compounds over time and eventually tanks rankings.

Before investing heavily in content or link building, ensure your technical foundation is solid. No point building on a cracked foundation.
